items.title: Fixed TTL expiration check to trigger file deletion on mounted points
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/5527

# How are we solving the problem?
Changing delete method calls in filer.go so that they also trigger a NotifyUpdateEvent and have a filer.remote.sync daemon simultaneously delete files on remote mounted point.

# How is the PR tested?
1. Start seaweed master/filer/volume docker images with patched exe, e.g.:
```
services:
  master:
    image: chrislusf/seaweedfs:local
    ports:
      - "9333:9333"
      - "19333:19333"
    command: "master -ip=master -ip.bind=0.0.0.0"
  volume:
    image: chrislusf/seaweedfs:local
    ports:
      - "8089:8080"
      - "18089:18080"
    command: 'volume -mserver="master:9333" -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8080'
    depends_on:
      - master
  filer:
    image: chrislusf/seaweedfs:local
    ports:
      - "8888:8888"
      - "18888:18888"
    command: 'filer -master="master:9333" -ip.bind=0.0.0.0'
    tty: true
    stdin_open: true
    depends_on:
      - master
      - volume
```
2. From weed shell:
    -  configure S3 credentials and mount some remote S3 bucket:
    ```
    > remote.configure -name=ttltest -type=s3 -s3.access_key=xxxx -s3.secret_key=yyyy -s3.storage_class=STANDARD -s3.region=eu-west-1
    > remote.mount -dir=/buckets/mytest -remote=ttltest/ttl-local-test
   ```
   - configure TTL on said bucket
   ```
   > fs.configure -locationPrefix=/buckets/mytest -ttl=1m -apply
   ```
3. Start a filer.remote.sync to sync filer updates to the bucket:
 ```
./weed filer.remote.sync -filer=localhost:8888 -dir=/buckets/mytest
```
4. Upload a random file to the bucket:
```
curl -F "file=@blah.txt" "http://localhost:8888/buckets/mytest/blah.txt
```
5. Wait for configured TTL to expire and execute fs.ls command from weed shell:
```
>fs.ls /buckets/mytest
```
6. Verify that file has been removed from filer *AND ALSO* deleted on remote /ttl-local-test S3 bucket.

items.title: feat: add UpdateVolumeLastModified RPC and implement timestamp logic
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

[see issues 6837](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/6837)

Currently, SeaweedFS calculates file TTL based on the file's creation time (Crtime), which is inconsistent with major cloud storage services (AWS S3, Alibaba Cloud OSS, Tencent Cloud COS) that use Last-Modified time. This creates several issues:

1. When a file is updated, users typically want the TTL countdown to restart
2. Creation time may not accurately reflect the actual lifecycle of a file
3. When a file is partially updated (e.g., split into chunks), some chunks might be prematurely expired due to TTL

# How are we solving the problem?

1. Added a new `UpdateVolumeLastModified` RPC interface to update volume's last modified time and make sure volume will not be expried. 
2. Modified the TTL calculation logic to use Mtime instead of Crtime
3. Implemented volume-level timestamp updates to handle partial file updates:
   - When a file is updated, we collect all volume IDs associated with the file's chunks
   - Call `UpdateVolumeLastModified` for each related volume
   - This ensures all chunks of a file have consistent TTL behavior
4. Updated protobuf definitions and storage backend interfaces to support the new timestamp logic
5. Added proper error handling and validation for timestamp updates
6.  Modified volume get interface to remove needle-level TTL checks:
   - Commented out needle TTL validation in volume get handler
   - Chunk deletion is now handled entirely by volume expiration
   - This ensures chunks are always returned when requested, regardless of their individual TTL status


# How is the PR tested?

1. Unit Tests:
2. Integration Tests:
   - Tested file updates with TTL
   - Tested UpdateVolumeLastModified` RPC interface works
   - Tested partial file updates
   - Tested TTL expiration
   - Tested backward compatibility

3. Manual Tests:
   - Verified TTL behavior with AWS S3 compatibility
   - Tested with different file sizes and chunk configurations
   - Verified timestamp updates in volume server logs

# Checks
- [ ] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

The implementation ensures that:
1. TTL behavior is consistent with major cloud storage services
2. Partial file updates don't cause premature chunk expiration

items.title: Change TTL Base from Creation Time to Modification Time
items.body:
## Current Behavior
Currently, SeaweedFS calculates file TTL based on the file's creation time (Crtime). This can be seen in the following code:

```go
if entry.TtlSec > 0 {
    if entry.Crtime.Add(time.Duration(entry.TtlSec) * time.Second).Before(time.Now()) {
        // handle expiration
    }
}
```

## Problem
1. Inconsistency with Major Cloud Storage Services:
   - AWS S3 uses Last-Modified time
   - Alibaba Cloud OSS uses Last-Modified time
   - Tencent Cloud COS uses Last-Modified time
   - And other major cloud storage services

2. Limited Use Cases:
   - When a file is updated, users typically want the TTL countdown to restart
   - Creation time may not accurately reflect the actual lifecycle of a file
   - For frequently updated files, using modification time is more reasonable

## Proposed Solutions

### Solution 1: Add TTL Strategy Support (Recommended)
Add flexibility to choose between creation time and modification time:

1. Add TTL Strategy Support:
   - Add a new field to specify TTL calculation strategy
   - Support both creation time and modification time
   - Allow configuration at both file level and path rule level

2. Implementation Approach:
   - Add TtlStrategy field to Entry structure
   - Update TTL check logic in filer and mount
   - Add TTL strategy to path rules
   - Ensure backward compatibility by treating zero value as creation time

### Solution 2: Simple Direct Change
A simpler approach that directly changes the TTL base to modification time:

```go
if entry.TtlSec > 0 {
    if entry.Mtime.Add(time.Duration(entry.TtlSec) * time.Second).Before(time.Now()) {
        // handle expiration
    }
}
```

## Impact Areas
1. Core Components:
   - Filer
   - Mount
   - Storage backends
   - Path rules (for Solution 1)

2. User Interface:
   - API changes (for Solution 1)
   - Configuration changes (for Solution 1)
   - Documentation updates

## Considerations

### Solution 1: TTL Strategy
1. Backward Compatibility:
   - Zero value of TtlStrategy will be treated as creation time
   - Existing data will continue to use creation time
   - New data can use modification time by default
   - No migration needed

2. Performance:
   - Minimal impact on existing operations
   - Small storage overhead for new field
   - No significant query performance impact

3. User Experience:
   - Clear documentation
   - Intuitive configuration
   - No migration required

### Solution 2: Simple Direct Change
1. Backward Compatibility:
   - This is a breaking change
   - Existing files will have their TTL expiration time changed
   - Users need to be aware of this change

2. Performance:
   - No performance impact
   - No storage overhead

3. User Experience:
   - Clear documentation about the change
   - Users need to review their TTL settings

## Next Steps
1. Discuss and choose between the two solutions
2. Create detailed implementation plan for the chosen solution
3. Implement and test changes
4. Update documentation
5. Release (as major version for Solution 2)

items.title: Filer access-time (atime) tracking for LRU eviction — design & PR roadmap
items.body:
## Summary

This issue tracks adding optional POSIX-style **access-time (`atime`)** tracking to
filer entries, so operators can evict cache entries by *least-recently-accessed* rather
than least-recently-modified/synced. It records the design and the sequence of small PRs
implementing it, so each PR can be reviewed as one step of an agreed plan.

The feature is **opt-in and defaults to `off`** — no behaviour changes unless an
operator enables it.

## Motivation

Filers fronting remote/cloud storage (the `remote.mount` + cache-eviction flow) need to
keep a local cache within a size budget by evicting the "oldest" entries. Today the only
available signal is `RemoteEntry.LastLocalSyncTsNs` (when the entry was cached), which is
a poor proxy for "oldest": a file cached once and then read thousands of times still
looks old and gets evicted, causing avoidable re-fetches. True LRU needs an access-time
signal, which the filer does not currently track.

## Design

- **`atime` field** on `FuseAttributes` (proto field tags 22/23 for seconds/nanos),
  serialized with the existing entry codec — entries are opaque protobuf blobs, so no
  per-backend migration is required.
- **Legacy fallback:** when an entry has no stored atime, reads fall back to `Mtime`
  (or `Crtime` if mtime is zero), so existing data is immediately sortable.
- **Update policy** (`off` | `relatime` | `strict`), modeled on POSIX mount options:
  - `off` (default) — never track.
  - `relatime` — only persist when the new atime is older than a threshold (default 24h)
    or older than mtime/ctime. Debounces writes.
  - `strict` — persist every forward-moving access.
  - Optional **path-prefix allow-list** to scope tracking to specific subtrees, matched
    at path-component boundaries (`/buckets/cache` matches `/buckets/cache/x` but not
    `/buckets/cache_backup/x`).
- **Persistence** goes through the canonical `Filer.UpdateEntry` path to keep
  inode/crtime invariants and metadata events consistent. Updates are explicitly
  best-effort (a concurrent write can clobber a bump); relatime debouncing keeps the
  race window small, and bumps only occur on read paths.
- **Read paths** bump atime via a fire-and-forget helper that coalesces duplicate
  `(dir, name)` requests within a flush window and short-circuits for background reads
  (replication, EC, prefetch, lifecycle) so those never affect atime.

## PR roadmap

| Step | Scope | PR | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Proto + codec foundation (`FuseAttributes.Atime`, `TouchAccessTime` RPC, init-from-mtime) | #9556 | ✅ Merged |
| 2a | `AtimePolicy` core (off/relatime/strict, path-prefix scoping) — pure logic + tests | #9898 | Open |
| 2b | `TouchAccessTime` server handler + `-atime*` flags (built on 2a) | #9583 | Draft until 2a merges |
| 3 | `weed/util/atime` client helper (coalescing Toucher, system-read bypass) — no wiring | _(planned)_ | — |
| 4 | Wire atime bumps into S3 / FUSE / WebDAV / Filer HTTP read paths | _(planned)_ | — |
| 5 | Surface atime in `weed shell fs.meta.cat` | _(planned)_ | — |

Each PR is intentionally kept small and self-contained. Feedback on the split
granularity or ordering is very welcome before I open the remaining ones.

items.title: Default collection keeps creating tiny volumes that never fill, using up all my volume slots
items.body:
## Problem

3-node cluster, replication 002, volumeSizeLimitMB=1000, filer without -collection (so filer logs go to the default collection).

The default collection now has ~53 volumes per server, each only 3–5 MB with ~300 files (less than 1% full). They all keep receiving small writes, but never fill up, and the master keeps creating new ones anyway.

Each volume uses a slot on all 3 servers, so I'm at 586/595 slots and can't grow volumes for my real collections anymore.

## What I tried

I tried consolidating with fs.mergeVolumes, then volume.vacuum -garbageThreshold=0.0001 and volume.deleteEmpty. This doesn't fully solve it: some files always remain in the volumes, so they are never completely empty and deleteEmpty can't remove them — the slots stay occupied.

Questions
Is this normal? Shouldn't the master reuse the existing nearly-empty volumes instead of creating new ones?
What's the recommended fix — [master.volume_growth] limits, weed filer -collection=..., or something else?
How can I fully empty and remove these small volumes to get my slots back, given that merge + vacuum leaves files behind?

## Environment

SeaweedFS 4.40, 3 nodes (master + volume + filer each), S3 gateway, admin + worker with default maintenance script, postgres2 filer store, -max=0 on volume servers.

items.title: SeaweedFS Filer Notification Multiple Webhooks
items.body:
Hi, I’m trying to configure multiple webhook notifications in SeaweedFS filer, but I’m unable to get it working and couldn’t find clear documentation on whether this is supported.
What I’m trying to achieve is I want to route events to different services based on path prefixes, similar to how MinIO supports multiple event targets:

Upload bucket (/data) → file-ingress
Asset bucket (/repository) → metadata-extractor

What I tried:
[notification.webhook.file_ingress]
enabled = true
endpoint = "{{ file_ingress_endpoint }}"
event_types = ["create"]
path_prefixes = ["/buckets/{{ seaweedfs_upload_bucket }}/data"]

[notification.webhook.metadata_extractor]
enabled = true
endpoint = "{{ metadata_extractor_endpoint }}"
event_types = ["create"]
path_prefixes = ["/buckets/{{ seaweedfs_asset_bucket }}/repository/"]

Observed behavior:

Using a single [notification.webhook] block works
But adding multiple webhook blocks:
Either only one works
Or events seem to stop being delivered properly
Resulting in downstream services (e.g., ingestion) not being triggered
Question:
Is it actually supported to define multiple webhook endpoints in SeaweedFS filer notifications?
If not, what is the recommended approach to:

Route events to multiple services?
Or implement fan-out (e.g., ingestion → metadata processing)?

items.title: s3api: enforce bucket lifecycle TTL on new volume assignments
items.body:
## Summary
- persist normalized bucket lifecycle TTL rules in bucket metadata
- pass resolved lifecycle TTL to AssignVolume in PutObject uploads
- set entry TtlSec from the same resolved lifecycle TTL for metadata consistency
- clear persisted lifecycle TTL rules when bucket lifecycle config is deleted
- add unit tests for lifecycle TTL rule encoding/decoding and longest-prefix matching

## Why
This removes the timing window where writes can be assigned to ttl=0 volumes before path-based filer config is fully visible, which was causing non-expiring objects after redeploy/recovery.

Fixes #8303


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Bucket lifecycle rules can define TTLs for automatic object expiration and are persisted with the bucket.
  * Objects uploaded to buckets inherit TTLs from the most specific matching lifecycle prefix.

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Requests with excessively large expiration values are rejected; failures saving lifecycle TTL configuration now return errors and are logged.

* **Tests**
  * Added unit tests covering TTL encoding/decoding and prefix-based TTL resolution.

items.title: S3 concurrent upload fails with "failed to write to replicas" and "context canceled" under load (v4.05)
items.body:
---

## Current situation

- **SeaweedFS version:** 4.05
- We use a custom S3 stress-test script that performs **concurrent uploads** of S3 objects (**100MB or 500MB** per object).
- **Cluster layout:** 5 machines; on each machine we run **master**, **volume**, **filer**, and **s3**; the first node also runs **admin**.

**Startup commands (one node shown; other nodes differ only by `-ip` / hostnames):**

```
# Master
/usr/bin/weed -logdir=/var/log/seaweedfs -v=0 master -ip=node1 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=9333 -metricsPort=9334 -mdir=/data -peers=ip1:9333,ip2:9333,ip3:9333,ip4:9333,ip5:9333 -volumeSizeLimitMB=1000 -defaultReplication=010 -garbageThreshold=0.3 -raftHashicorp=true

# Volume
/usr/bin/weed -logdir=/var/log/seaweedfs -v=0 volume -ip=node1 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8080 -metricsPort=9335 -dir=/data -max=0 -fileSizeLimitMB=1000 -master=ip1:9333,ip2:9333,ip3:9333,ip4:9333,ip5:9333 -dataCenter=dc-ssd -rack=rackB-ssd -minFreeSpace=1

# Filer
/usr/bin/weed -logdir=/var/log/seaweedfs -v=0 filer -ip=node1 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8888 -metricsPort=9385 -master=node1:9333,node2:9333,node3:9333,node4:9333,node5:9333 -maxMB=4 -defaultStoreDir=/data

# S3
/usr/bin/weed -logdir=/var/log/seaweedfs -v=0 s3 -filer=node1:8888,node2:8888,node3:8888,node4:8888,node5:8888 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8333 -metricsPort=9389 -config=/etc/seaweedfs/s3config.json -iam=false -allowDeleteBucketNotEmpty=false
```
---

## Problem description

**From the benchmark tool:**

```
2026/02/24 13:48:03 upload part bench-on-01/db5e55c0e96a-100m-uniq part 2 failed: XMinioBackendDown: Remote backend is unreachable (Put "http://node1:8333/bench-on-01/955a7dcf94fc45a4a21d5e1acc50fef62": net/http: timeout awaiting response headers)
```

So the benchmark client reports that **one node’s S3 endpoint (node1:8333) is unreachable**: the Put request did not receive response headers before the client’s timeout (“timeout awaiting response headers”). We suspect **request/task backlog** under concurrency is causing the benchmark to fail. However, **cluster machines do not appear to be at their physical limits** (CPU/memory/disk). We would like to ask:

- **What is the root cause here?** Is it that our **startup parameters need tuning**, or that the **cluster has hit a physical bottleneck**?
- **How can we confirm** which of these it is?

**From SeaweedFS side we also see:**

1. **S3 (weed s3) logs:** Uploads to volume servers fail with **"failed to write to replicas for volume XXX"** and **"Post \"...?type=replicate\": context canceled"**. Chunked upload then fails and orphan chunks are cleaned up.
2. **Volume server logs:** Replication POSTs to other volume nodes fail with **"context canceled"**, and the volume returns **HTTP 500** with a JSON error body. So replica writes are being canceled when the incoming request’s context is canceled (e.g. client or upstream timeout).

We suspect **replication is tied to the incoming HTTP request context**: when that context is canceled, replica uploads are canceled too, leading to "failed to write to replicas" and S3 failures. We are unsure whether this is expected behavior or something that should be changed, and whether startup options can reduce the issue.

---

## Questions

1. Is the **replica write** in `store_replicate.go` intentionally using the **incoming HTTP request context**? When that context is canceled (e.g. client disconnect or upstream timeout), replication POSTs get "context canceled" and we see 500 and S3 failures. Under concurrent load this happens frequently. Would it make sense to use a **detached context** (e.g. with a timeout) for replica uploads so replication can complete even if the original request is canceled?

2. Besides fixing or tuning that behavior, are there **recommended startup options** for S3/volume/filer under high concurrency (e.g. `-idleTimeout`, `-concurrentUploadLimitMB`, volume/filer limits) that could reduce timeouts and "failed to write to replicas"?

3. How can we **confirm whether the bottleneck is** (a) client/load-balancer timeouts, (b) S3/volume/filer configuration, or (c) disk/network on the nodes? Any suggested metrics (e.g. from `-metricsPort`) or logs to check?

---

## Additional context

- Replication is **010** (one replica); each write is sent to one other volume node.
- Chunk size in the flow is **8388608 bytes** (8 MiB).
- Failures occur during **concurrent** S3 multipart uploads (100MB / 500MB objects).
- Cluster resources (CPU, memory, disk) do not appear saturated when the errors occur.

Thanks in advance for any guidance or possible fixes.

items.title: Lazily-created remote-mount entries carry no TTL and accumulate without bound
items.body:
All references are to `master` @ `db5a086d0` (4.41).

## Problem

Under a lazy remote mount, filer entries are created on demand: `maybeLazyFetchFromRemote` on a miss in `FindEntry` (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote.go:30-117`) and `maybeLazyListFromRemote` on a directory listing (`weed/filer/filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:32-173`). Both create remote-only mappings — a path pointing at an object in the remote store — and neither sets `TtlSec`, so it stays `0` and nothing ever expires them.

They therefore accumulate one entry per distinct object ever touched, and are never reclaimed. On one of our filers that is currently **11,142,152 entries, growing by roughly 330,000/day**, with no upper bound short of the object count of the bucket.

The mount's own cache TTL does not help: `ListingCacheTtlSeconds` only decides how often a directory is re-listed from the remote (`filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:60-76`), and re-listing an existing entry takes the merge path at `:107-120`, which updates it. Nothing removes anything.

This is a real operational ceiling for anyone fronting cloud storage with a shared filer store. The entries are trivially reconstructible — the remote is authoritative, and a filer that lacks an entry re-derives it on the next access via exactly the code that created it.

## Why plain TTL is the right mechanism

The filer already has expiry machinery that does precisely what a cache wants, and — importantly — the *plain* TTL path never touches the remote:

- `FindEntry`: `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry(ctx, entry)` then `ErrNotFound` (`weed/filer/filer.go:434-437`);
- `doListDirectoryEntries`: expired entries collected at `:473-476` and deleted via `f.Store.DeleteOneEntry` at `:496-500`.

Both go to the store and nothing else. Neither reaches `doDeleteEntryMetaAndData`, so `maybeDeleteFromRemote` — which is gated on `!isFromOtherCluster` inside it (`weed/filer/filer_delete_entry.go:144-152`) — is not on that code path at all. Expiring a cached entry **cannot** propagate a delete to the remote object.

Worth having on the record: the S3-lifecycle branch a few lines above behaves differently. It calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, entry, true, false, nil)` (`filer.go:429` and `:492`) with `isFromOtherCluster: false`, so it *does* reach `maybeDeleteFromRemote` and *does* propagate. Whatever is decided here, those two expiry paths are not interchangeable for remote-mounted content.

No new job, no sweep, no schedule — the reclamation is already written.

## Two things have to be fixed first

### 1. `Crtime` is stamped with the remote object's mtime

Both creation sites set `Crtime` to the remote mtime, not to the creation time:

- `filer_lazy_remote.go:84-95` — `mtime := time.Unix(remoteEntry.RemoteMtime, 0)`, then `Mtime: mtime, Crtime: mtime`;
- `filer_lazy_remote_listing.go:137-146` — same, defaulting to `time.Now()` only when `RemoteMtime` is absent.

The expiry check is `Crtime + TtlSec < now`. Stamping a TTL as the code stands would expire every object older than the TTL window the instant its entry is created. And in `FindEntry` the expiry branch `return`s at `filer.go:436`, before the lazy-fetch fallback at `:440-446` — so the caller gets `ErrNotFound` for an object that demonstrably exists in the remote. The next request re-creates the entry, which is immediately expired again: objects would alternate 200/404 forever.

So `Crtime` has to mean "when this entry was created", with `Mtime` keeping the remote mtime. That split is arguably just correct on its own merits, independent of TTLs — `Crtime` is currently reporting a fact about the remote object rather than about the entry, and `entryInitialAtime` (`filer.go:395-400`) already prefers `Mtime` where the distinction matters.

### 2. Expiring a directory's last child can delete the remote prefix

This one I did not expect, and it is the reason I am opening an issue rather than a PR.

The entry deletion itself is store-only, as above. But `doListDirectoryEntries` does not stop there — when the expiry pass leaves no valid entries it calls `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` (`filer.go:502-507`), and that path *does* propagate:

- `IsDirectoryEmpty` (`filer.go:585-592`) calls `f.Store.ListDirectoryPrefixedEntries` directly, bypassing `maybeLazyListFromRemote` — so it sees only the local store and reports the directory empty even though every object is still sitting in the remote;
- it then calls `f.doDeleteEntryMetaAndData(ctx, dirEntry, false, false, nil)` (`filer.go:573-574`) — `isFromOtherCluster: false`;
- for a directory entry, `maybeDeleteFromRemote` calls `client.RemoveDirectory` (`filer_lazy_remote.go:139-148`);
- `RemoveDirectory` on S3 (`weed/remote_storage/s3/s3_storage_client.go:429`) and GCS (`weed/remote_storage/gcs/gcs_storage_client.go:222`) lists the prefix and **deletes every object under it**.

The only guard is the depth check at `filer.go:550-555`, which protects `/buckets/<bucket>` but nothing below it. So a TTL on lazy entries, added naively, turns "this directory's cached metadata went cold" into "wipe that prefix from the bucket".

It is latent today only because lazy entries carry `TtlSec: 0` and so never reach that code. (The same `isFromOtherCluster: false` call is reachable from the scheduled empty-folder cleaner — `weed/filer/empty_folder_cleanup/empty_folder_cleaner.go:360` — which suggests the interaction between remote mounts and empty-directory cleanup deserves a look regardless of this proposal.)

The fix that fits the existing design is to make `maybeDeleteFromRemote` decline to remove a directory whose emptiness was never confirmed against the remote, or to skip `DeleteEmptyParentDirectories` when the entries were reclaimed by cache expiry rather than deleted by a client. I would rather agree the shape with you than pick one.

## Proposal

Three parts:

1. `Crtime` = creation time at both lazy-creation sites, `Mtime` unchanged. Small and independently defensible.
2. Do not propagate a remote directory removal that originates from cache expiry (see above).
3. Give lazy-created entries a configurable TTL.

For (3), the machinery already exists and I would rather reuse it than add a flag: `FilerConf.PathConf.ttl` (`weed/pb/filer.proto:758`) is already parsed by `needle.ReadTTL` and turned into the entry's `TtlSec` on the upload path (`weed/server/filer_server_handlers_write.go:289-295`). Having the two lazy-creation sites do the same `f.FilerConf.MatchStorageRule(path).GetTtl()` lookup would mean a lazy mount is configured with the command that already exists:

```
fs.configure -locationPrefix=/buckets/mybucket/ -ttl=7d -apply
```

no new proto field, no new flag, and it composes with everything else `filer.conf` already scopes per path. The alternative — a `remote.mount -entryTTL` flag mirroring `-listingCacheTTL` (`weed/shell/command_remote_mount.go:73,93`) — keeps the setting next to the mount it belongs to, at the cost of a second place TTLs come from. I lean towards the `filer.conf` route but have no strong attachment.

## Related

Under a store that expires values natively, there is a second half to this. `redis2`'s directory index leaks a member for every entry whose value key expires, because the listing loop only cleans up on the logical-expiry branch and not on the not-found branch that TTL entries actually take — so TTL-based reclamation frees the values but not the index. Fix in #10735. The two changes compose: TTLs here, and a store that stays clean when they fire.

Background: #8391, #8454, #8522, #8568 are the lazy remote-mount work this builds on. Happy to implement all three parts if the approach sounds right — particularly keen for a steer on (2) before writing anything.

items.title: TTL Attribute Lost When Editing Files with Vim in Weed Mount
items.body:
## Describe the bug
When using vim editor to modify files in a SeaweedFS filesystem mounted via weed mount, the TTL (Time To Live) attribute of the files is lost. This issue affects scenarios where maintaining file TTL attributes is crucial, such as temporary file or cache file management.

## Steps to reproduce
1. Start SeaweedFS service
2. Mount the filesystem using weed mount command
3. Create a file with TTL attribute, for example:
   ```bash
   curl -F  test.txt xxx http://localhost:8888/logs/test.txt?ttl=10m
   ```
4. Edit the file using vim editor:
   ```bash
   vim logs/test.txt
   ```
5. Save and exit vim
6. Check the file's TTL attribute:
   ```bash
   curl   xxx http://localhost:8888/logs/test.txt?metadata=true
   ```

## Expected behavior
The TTL attribute should remain unchanged after editing the file with vim, maintaining consistency with the original settings.

## Actual behavior
After editing the file, the TTL attribute is cleared, and the file becomes permanent (without TTL restriction).

items.title: filer: format adapters align storage chunks to file structure (HLS TS, parquet)
items.body:
This generalizes the idea in #10658. Instead of an HLS-specific virtual namespace, the filer gets a small format adapter system: an adapter reduces one container format to extent sizes, an alignment quantum, and an opaque payload. The core never learns what a TS packet or a row group is, and adapters never see chunks, file ids, or authorization. HLS TS and parquet ship as the first two adapters.

## Why align chunks to file structure

The chunk is the unit of lookup, caching, CRC, EC recovery, and tiering. When chunk boundaries coincide with the file's internal structure, a segment or row-group read maps to exactly its covering chunks: one lookup and one volume round trip instead of two, whole-needle reads that verify CRC, caches that hold exactly the hot bytes, and half the fan-out on EC and cloud-tiered volumes. Arbitrary fixed-size cuts give none of that when readers fetch sub-ranges.

## How it works

The upload loop now accepts a boundary source instead of a fixed chunk size; the fixed size stays as the default implementation. A `Layout` (extent sizes + align + adapter payload) is derived by the adapter and drives the cuts: chunks never span extents, extents larger than `maxMB` split on the align quantum. The layout persists in one compact `x-seaweedfs-` extended attribute, keyed by extent sizes rather than chunk ids so it survives chunk manifest folding — about 3 bytes per extent.

Everything runs on the entry's real path, so JWT prefix scopes, WORM, and read-only rules apply unchanged. No new namespace, no auth bypass knob, no config.

- `POST /path?format.ingest=hls-ts` ingests a multipart `index` sidecar (the FFmpeg-generated EXT-X-BYTERANGE playlist) plus the `media` bytes, cutting chunks on segment boundaries at 188-byte packet alignment.
- `GET /path?format.view=hls-ts` serves a rewritten playlist with plain numbered segment URLs for clients that do not speak byte-range HLS; `&seq=N` streams one segment through the normal prefetch path with entry ETag, preconditions, and HEAD.
- `POST /path?format.repack=parquet` derives the layout from the stored bytes (parquet keeps its index in the footer, so ingest-time cutting is impossible) and rewrites the chunks cut at row-group starts, swapping the entry and queueing the old chunks for deletion. Parquet needs no view; readers already fetch row groups by offset, alignment alone delivers the benefit.

```
ffmpeg -i input.mp4 ... -f hls -hls_playlist_type vod -hls_flags single_file \
  -hls_segment_filename video.ts index.m3u8

curl -F 'index=@index.m3u8' -F 'media=@video.ts;type=video/mp2t' \
  'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.ingest=hls-ts'
curl 'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.view=hls-ts'          # playlist
curl 'http://filer:8888/videos/movie.ts?format.view=hls-ts&seq=0'    # segment

curl -X POST 'http://filer:8888/data/part-0001.parquet?format.repack=parquet'
```

## Boundaries that keep it maintainable

Adapters implement identity plus whatever capabilities fit (`Sniffer`, `Indexer`, `SidecarIndexer`, `Viewer`) and are discovered by type assertion; they register from `init()` like filer stores. Viewers return a plan (a rendered document or an extent number) and the server executes it, so streaming stays on the optimized path and adapters stay pure functions. A `formattest` kit holds every adapter to no-panic parsing of truncated input, since indexers parse untrusted bytes inside a storage daemon.

The layout is advisory: a stale or corrupt one 404s its views while plain reads stay untouched. It is also bound to a digest of the chunk list it described, so a write through any other path (offset writes, appends, mounts) invalidates the views until re-ingest or repack, even when the file size is unchanged.

## Limitations

- Repack refuses hard-linked, remote, and server-side-encrypted entries. Versioned entries are fine: every object version owns its chunk list. Within a filer, writes serialize on the per-path entry lock - gRPC writers, renames, plain-HTTP overwrites, and repack all take it, and WORM is revalidated under it. The lock is filer-local, so repack also re-reads the entry from the store at commit time and aborts with 409 if anything that fed the repack changed - chunk fingerprint, file size, TTL and both expiry anchors, the S3-expiry flag, hard-link or remote state - or WORM was enabled. The cross-filer window shrinks to the swap itself, inside which repack races like any ordinary writer. Closing it entirely needs owner routing like the S3 gateway's, which is the follow-up; until then route writes for a path to one filer. TTL'd entries repack with their remaining lifetime, anchored the way expiry actually works (Mtime for S3-expiring entries, Crtime otherwise) and rounded up to a volume-representable TTL so chunks never expire before their entry.
- Ingest is explicit; nothing sniffs uploads on the write path.
- S3 surface (per-bucket repack policy, align hints on PUT) and a background repack worker are follow-ups; this PR is the storage and serving foundation they build on.

Tests cover the layout codec and cutter, playlist parsing/rendering/rejections, parquet extent derivation against footer metadata, truncation fuzzing for both adapters, and the full existing weed/server suite passes.

items.title: filer.remote.sync and filer.remote.gateway failing to upload large 300mb and larger files to azure blob storage
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
Large files (over 300MB) very often failing to write back to azure blob storage using `weed filer.remote.sync` or `weed filer.remote.gataway` operations.
after some time we are getting "context deadline exceeded"

also those commands are causing high latency and client-side errors on azure blob storage

Office where k8s cluster is running has 2 x 1GB internet lines, so connection is not the issue. 
Uploading same files using azure storage explorer is fast and reliable. 
 
**System Setup**
Seaweed is deployed on k8s cluster 1.27.1 using seaweedfs helm chart from the github repository. 

- List the command line to start 

1 master statefulset pod
"weed master", `weed -logtostderr=true -v=1 master -port=9333 -mdir=/data -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -defaultReplication=001 -metricsPort=9327 -volumeSizeLimitMB=30000 -garbageThreshold=0.3 -ip=seaweedfs-master-0.seaweedfs-master.seaweedfs -peers=seaweedfs-master-0.seaweedfs-master.seaweedfs:9333`

3 volume statefulset pods
"weed volume", `weed -logtostderr=true -v=1 volume -port=8080 -metricsPort=9327 -dir=/data -max=0 -rack=nbs-k8s -dataCenter=nbs -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -readMode=proxy -fileSizeLimitMB=1024 -minFreeSpacePercent=7 -ip=seaweedfs-volume-0.seaweedfs-volume.seaweedfs -compactionMBps=50 -mserver=seaweedfs-master-0.seaweedfs-master.seaweedfs:9333`

1 filer statefulset pod
"weed filer", `weed -logtostderr=true -v=1 filer -port=8888 -metricsPort=9327 -dirListLimit=100000 -ip=10.233.74.158 -master=seaweedfs-master-0.seaweedfs-master.seaweedfs:9333`

3 S3 Replicaset pods
"weed s3", `weed -logdir=/logs -v=1 s3 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8333 -metricsPort 9327 -allowEmptyFolder=true -filer=seaweedfs-filer-client.seaweedfs:8888`

- OS version
```
/data # cat /etc/os-release
NAME="Alpine Linux"
ID=alpine
VERSION_ID=3.19.0
PRETTY_NAME="Alpine Linux v3.19"
```
- output of `weed version`
`version 30GB 3.61 8ae00e47a linux amd64`
issue happens and with the latest seaweedfs 3.62 version when I was testing it on the local computer and running this seaweedfs command:
`weed server -filer -s3 -volume.max=0 -dir ./data`

- if using filer, show the content of `filer.toml`
```
/data # cat /etc/seaweedfs/filer.toml
[leveldb2]
enabled = true
dir = "/data/filerldb2"
```

**Expected behavior**
large files being written back to azure blob when running `weed filer.remote.sync` or `weed filer.remote.gateway` commands

**screenshots**
![image](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/assets/85372149/eb1653a2-7d62-4193-9bf2-2fa6e46d8ea0)


**Additional context**
Log entry from `weed filer.remote.gateway` command when it fails to write large file:
```
{"log":"{\"log\":\"Put \\\"https://storage_account_name.blob.core.windows.net/container/folder/largefile.pq?blockid=uVVM8kDrRSpHZHtuCYqybg%3D%3D\\u0026comp=block\\u0026timeout=61\\\": context deadline exceeded\\n\",\"stream\":\"stderr\",\"time\":\"2024-01-23T05:34:07.910887979Z\"}","kubernetes_pod_name":"seaweedfs-helper-5598d784c6-pv2r4","kubernetes_namespace_name":"seaweedfs","kubernetes_pod_id":"5c09b09c-cf4e-41e3-97b2-7143bc7ef279","kubernetes_labels":{"app":"seaweedfs","component":"helper","pod-template-hash":"5598d784c6","release":"seaweedfs"},"kubernetes_annotations":{"cni.projectcalico.org/containerID":"f7f229387f467e250769f3750d1ca0b0eb023bc665a8cfe398507637ba6cb702","cni.projectcalico.org/podIP":"10.233.125.143/32","cni.projectcalico.org/podIPs":"10.233.125.143/32"},"kubernetes_host":"nbs-k8s-worker-3","kubernetes_container_name":"seaweed-writeback","kubernetes_docker_id":"4b68496f8d0d537946b5204bb32b78ba38bb2c81815dd124f3868ac18acd9cb4","kubernetes_container_hash":"chrislusf/seaweedfs@sha256:a947f24b3fafaafab5fe249286787739f10e7f02b7ed2c392bbccf9ecf0415a9","kubernetes_container_image":"chrislusf/seaweedfs:latest","cluster":"nbs01-ks01"}
```

- master,volume,filer and s3 are different processes

weed master -disableHttp -volumeSizeLimitMB=10240  -volumePreallocate=false  -mdir=/seaweedfs/mdir
weed volume -dataCenter=dc -dir=/seaweedfs/volume -dir.idx=/seaweedfs/index -max=0

weed -logdir /var/log/seaweedfs filer.sync -a filer1:8888 -b filer2:8888

items.title: # Proposal: Filer Support for Volume-ID Reverse Index and Batch Cleanup
items.body:
we'd like your input first, thanks!

Before submitting the full implementation, **we would first like to know whether upstream recommends an officially sanctioned alternative approach** — if a lighter-weight or more generic mechanism already exists, we will adopt it over our own implementation. Points we've already investigated but have open questions about:

1. **After `weed shell volume.delete`, what does upstream recommend for cleaning up stale Filer references?**
   - Is there an existing command/endpoint we've missed (e.g. some path in volume.vacuum, a `fs.*` family command)?
   - Would upstream recommend an alternative strategy such as "periodic full `fs.meta.save` + rebuild" or "GC scan"?

2. **The retry storm in the Filer deletion queue after volume deletion** (`no deletion result for retried file` flooding):
   - Does upstream suggest solving this via `MaxRetryAttempts` or a config knob, rather than us changing the code directly?

3. **Reverse-lookup of files by volume — does upstream have other ideas?**
   - For example: scanning the Filer leveldb **directly by `FileId` prefix** (instead of our separate `_vid_idx` index database)?
   - Or does upstream consider that this scenario should not be handled by the Filer at all — instead the **application should delete files before deleting the volume**?

4. **If upstream agrees with the direction**: should the reverse index be a **generic store capability** (all backends), or is a leveldb2-only minimal implementation acceptable?

> If upstream has a better approach, we will adopt it; 

---

## 1. Background & Problem

In a single-node SeaweedFS deployment, we use a **watchdog that periodically deletes volumes** (TTL expiry + disk/volume-count trigger) to control storage water level.
After deleting a volume, two serious problems arise:

1. **Ghost files remain**: After a volume is deleted, the Filer still holds `FileChunk` entries referencing those volumes.
   The Filer's leveldb store has **no way to reverse-lookup "which file references volume X"** — the only option is a full directory-tree scan, which takes hours to days at the 50-million-file scale and is practically unusable.

2. **Log flooding**: After a volume is deleted, the Filer's internal deletion tasks keep retrying against the now-missing volume (`no deletion result for retried file`),
   ~10 retries each with exponential backoff up to 6 hours, flooding the logs.

Upstream `weed shell volume.delete` only removes the physical volume — it does **not** clean up the Filer metadata references,
and provides no interface to look up "files" from a "volume". We therefore implemented this **volume_id reverse index** mechanism.

---

## 2. Goals

- **Second-level cleanup after volume deletion**: use volume id to reverse-lookup and delete all Filer entries referencing that volume (data + index).
- **Automatic empty-directory cleanup**: once files are deleted, the parent-directory chain is checked bottom-up and removed if empty — no empty shell directories left behind.
- **Low overhead on the hot path**: index maintenance during normal upload/overwrite/delete should not significantly increase I/O 
- **Expose an HTTP interface**: for external orchestration (watchdog, S3 lifecycle, trash/recycle, etc.).

---

items.title: Implement `VolumeEcShardsGenerateStreaming()`, a streaming version of the `VolumeEcShardsGenerate()` gRPC.
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/9336

# How are we solving the problem?

Implement a streaming version of `VolumeEcShardsGenerate()`.  For large volumes, this operation can take a significant amount of time, so streaming progress updates a useful keepalive indicator for clients.

This PR does not overwrite `VolumeEcShardsGenerate()`, but implements a **new** gRPC call instead `VolumeEcShardsGenerateStreaming()`, to guarantee API backwards compatibility. Not sure if this
is required thou, given that both clients and servers are expected to run the same `weed` command.

# How is the PR tested?

No functional changes.

items.title: enable faster vacuuming with concurrency
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
Due to the single threaded nature of the vacuum implementation, it is possible for high write volume clusters with low TTLs to be unable to actually evict the cache contents at a rate the operator desires.

# How are we solving the problem?
Utilize all existing volume vacuum logic but enable it to run on multiple volumes at the same time via a go routine worker pool. The pool size can be grown via a flag.

# How is the PR tested?
Set the flag to >1 and both logs and disk usage metrics will show the system is able to vacuum multiple volumes at a time such that the garbage collection and compaction can occur much quicker.

# Checks
- [ ] ~I have added unit tests if possible.~ - **This code relies on existing unit tests as it wraps an existing implementation.**
- [x] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

items.body:
Hi!
I have a feature request for an `-azure.endpoint` flag to specify an endpoint when using `remote.configure` command on a remote **azure blob storage** in `weed shell`.
The main usage would be to be able to use seaweedfs gateway on azure blob endpoints that are **not** hosted by https://*.blob.core.windows.net.

items.title: ♻️ refactor(worker): follow CSP model
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

After removing mutex use by creating a state manager, fundamental problems of state-oriented concurrency vs CSP-model based concurrency remained (such as polling instead of reacting to events, maintaining a lot of state, unclear lifecycles and overly complicated and error-prone logic for connecting, starting, stopping etc.). With this refactor, the state managers are completely removed and relevant processes communicate with each other directly through channels. Provides clean connection logic, clean starting and stopping logic, and clearly demarcated architecture, since the channels now define the structure instead of overloaded actions. 

Overall, provides a good base for further feature development on workers such as cancellation of tasks. 

# How are we solving the problem?

Removing the manager loop and examining which state is actually necessary vs historical code baggage. We end up with no shared state between concurrent processes.

# How is the PR tested?

There is still no mock interface to facilitate simple testing, but a proper dependency injection-minded worker constructur (NewWorker) is a starting point.

# Checks
- [ ] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

* **Refactor**
  * Worker lifecycle rewritten to an event-driven, channel-based model with clearer error propagation, signal-driven graceful shutdown, asynchronous task handling, and removal of legacy command/polling loops.
  * Connection and task flows reworked to reactive processes with exponential backoff reconnects, streamlined heartbeat/task requests, and removal of per-task working-directory creation.

* **New Features**
  * Exposed observable connection event stream and simplified admin client creation.
  * Public entry to start a worker from configuration.

items.title: Problem with filer event notification streams
items.body:
Hi
**Describe the bug**
I was trying to subscribe to the filer event notification via its gRPC port. The situation is that when the seaweedFS is idle and nothing interacts with it, when I subscribe to it for e.g 5 hours ago, it will stream the whole events from 5 hours ago. but the problem is that when it reaches the end of the stream and while seaweedFS is idle it won't close the stream and I have to set a timeout for the whole stream connection. But interestingly when I start to interact with seaweedFS which leads to new events, it would close my last connection for event notifications and I have to subscribe for the events again.
Another behavior which caught my attention was that when i am trying to subscribe to the filer while its under heavy read and writes unstoppable, each time i subscribe to the filer it will send me all events till now and then closes the stream, and i have to subscribe to it one more time. but when it reaches to the end of heavy interactions with seaweedFS and makes it idle, then it will show me all events since now and then won't close the connection and leaves it open till a new event happens.      

**System Setup**
On k8s
1 master -> `weed master -mdir=/data/seaweedfs/master -ip=weed-master-svc -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -defaultReplication=001 -volumeSizeLimitMB 100  -metricsPort=9324`
2 volume servers -> `weed volume -dir=/data/seaweedfs/volume -dataCenter=dc1  -rack=rack1 -mserver=weed-master-svc:9333 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -port=8080 -max=0 -metricsPort=9325`
1 filer -> `weed filer -master=weed-master-svc:9333 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -metricsPort=9326`
1 filer db which is scyllaDB
1 S3 instance -> `weed s3 -config=/conf/config.json -filer=weed-filer-svc:8888 -ip.bind=0.0.0.0 -metricsPort=9327`
**Expected behavior**
I can't understand the logic and behavior of event notification streams. They are open when seaweedFS is idle and they will close when a new event happens. Also why filer shows the events till now and closes the connection when there are ongoing events and then I subscribe to them.
**Additional context**
This issue is kinda connected to my other issue: [ filer.backup synchronisation with a external minio S3](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/4977)

items.title: FUSE returns empty file on cold cache read from S3 remote storage
items.body:
# Problem
When reading a file for the first time from a `weed mount` FUSE filesystem, if the file is not present in SeaweedFS locally and needs to be fetched from a remote S3 backend, the `read()` system call returns immediately with a buffer of null bytes. The command (e.g., `cat`) therefore outputs an empty file.

This initial read operation correctly triggers the file to be downloaded from S3 and stored locally in the background. Any subsequent attempt to read the same file succeeds and returns the correct content.

This suggests the FUSE client is not blocking to wait for the S3 download to complete before returning from the `read()` call.

# Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount a S3 bucket to the Filer
2. Use SeaweedFS CSI driver to mount path in Filer to pod
3. Ensure file not in SeaweedFS cache (`remote.uncache`)
4. From the pod, execute `cat /path/to/mounted/file`
5. **Observe**: command completes instantly with no output
6. Immediately execute `cat /path/to/mounted/file` again
7. **Observe**: command now correctly outputs the full content of the file

# Expected Behaviour
The first cat `/path/to/mounted/file` command should block until the file content is fully downloaded from S3 so that the correct file can be output on the first read attempt.

# Evidence
Using `strace`, we can see the `read()` call returns the correct number of bytes, but the buffer is filled with nulls on a cold cache.

**Cold Cache** `strace`:
The read call returns a buffer of `\0` bytes:
```

```

items.title: glog: add in-memory ring buffer with log interceptor
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a new `weed/logbuffer` package that captures every glog line into a thread-safe circular ring buffer for runtime log querying and live streaming.

### What's included:

- **LogInterceptor hook** in `glog.output()` — zero-cost when disabled (nil check)
- **Ring buffer** — fixed-capacity circular buffer with `sync.RWMutex` for concurrent read/write safety
- **Dual-mode parser** — auto-detects JSON (`--log_json`) vs classic glog text format
- **Atomic stats counters** — lock-free per-level counts (INFO/WARNING/ERROR/FATAL), total written, dropped
- **Fan-out subscribers** — non-blocking channel delivery for SSE streaming, with drop counting for slow consumers
- **Query engine** — filter by level, time range, file glob, regex pattern, request_id; supports pagination (offset + limit)
- **Utility methods** — `RecentErrors(n)`, `TopFiles(n)`, `ErrorRate(window)`
- **Runtime verbosity control** — `GetVerbosity`/`SetVerbosity`/`GetVModule`/`SetVModule` + `SetVerbosityWithTTL` for temporary debug verbosity that auto-reverts

### Design decisions:

- Buffer initialized after `flag.Parse()` so `--log_json` is resolved
- `LogInterceptor` is a simple `func(int32, []byte)` — no interface, no allocation
- Parser uses `raw[0] == '{'` for O(1) format detection
- All stats use `sync/atomic` for lock-free reads from HTTP handlers

### Files changed:

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `weed/glog/glog.go` | +LogInterceptor var, hook in output(), +Get/SetVerbosity, +Get/SetVModule |
| `weed/logbuffer/entry.go` | Log entry types and filter/query/stats structs |
| `weed/logbuffer/ring.go` | Ring buffer: Write, Query, Subscribe, Stats, RecentErrors, TopFiles, ErrorRate |
| `weed/logbuffer/parser.go` | Dual-mode log line parser (JSON + text) |
| `weed/logbuffer/global.go` | Global singleton, Init(), SetVerbosityWithTTL |
| `weed/logbuffer/ring_test.go` | 29 unit tests + 3 benchmarks |
| `weed/logbuffer/parser_test.go` | 16 unit tests |
| `weed/weed.go` | +logbuffer.Init(10000) after flag.Parse() |

## Test plan

- [x] `go test ./weed/logbuffer/` — 29 ring buffer tests + 16 parser tests pass
- [x] `go test ./weed/glog/` — existing glog tests unaffected
- [x] `go build ./weed/` — full binary compiles
- [x] `go vet ./weed/glog/ ./weed/logbuffer/` — no issues
- [ ] CI cross-platform validation

items.body: Hi. I'm trying to setup a cluster for http live streaming(hls, dash). Usage pattern - high rate upload, rewrite and delete requests(basic http PUT/DELETE via filer, s3 not needed). Configured 3x(master + volume + filer) identical nodes. HW: 2x Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 5420+, 512Gb RAM, 2x960Gb nvme(in raid1) for OS, master/filer data and volumes index 2x960Gb nvme(in raid1) for volumes data, fs - ext4. items.title: Negative number of free volumes, grow fails, system stalls
items.body:
We have a system with 3 masters, and 3 volumes. Running on version 3.85. Replication 001.

The system has become crowded, and two disk have been filling up to the max, becoming read only.

We therefore added two more servers being both masters and volumes, each 30 TB in size.

However, new data can still not be added.

`curl http://localhost:9333/vol/grow?count=4&dataNode={new volume server}`

gives

`{"error":"only -103972 volumes left, not enough for 8"}`

Calling

`curl http://localhost:9333/dir/assign`

gives

`{"error":"failed to find writable volumes for collection: replication:001 ttl: error: No writable volumes and no free volumes left for {\"replication\":{\"node\":1},\"ttl\":{\"Count\":0,\"Unit\":0},\"preallocate\":1073741824}"}`

The system now is down

items.title: Support glob pattern for path specific configuration
items.body:
Hi there,

We are evaluating using Seaweed as an S3 replacement for an on-prem product. 
First, this is a great project and it works really good for us so thanks for that! We are now trying to see how we can keep current behavior for files TTL as we have in our cloud.

To be more specific, we want to be able to configure TTL for such paths: `/buckets/my-buckets/prefix/*/data/*`. This is just an example for a path such as `/buckets/my-bucket/prefix/{dynamicValue}/data/`

As I have tested so far I see the current support for path-specific configuration is for prefix path only, and not for glob patterns (as the name indeed imply: `locationPrefix`).

Is there an option to extend the configuration also for patterns? perhaps adding an option to define `locationPattern` instead of `locationPrefix`? or support it somehow in the current config?

I have looked at the code doing the matching in `filer_conf.go` - `MatchStorageRule` function, and I'm not sure how we can modify current code to easily support it without breaking current behavior.
Maybe someone have an idea how we can support such a feature ?

Thank you!

items.title: Path-Specific TTL Applies to Directories, Leading to Premature Deletion and Inaccessible Files
items.body:
**Describe the bug:**

When configuring a Time-To-Live (TTL) using `fs.configure` with a specific `locationPrefix`, the TTL is applied not only to files but also to directories. This behavior results in directories being deleted before their contained files have expired, rendering the files inaccessible through the file system interface.

**Steps to reproduce:**

1. Set a TTL for a specific path prefix:

   ```bash
   fs.configure -locationPrefix=/logs/ -ttl=10m -apply
   ```



2. Create a directory  to the configured path:

   ```bash
   curl http://localhost:8888/logs/test/
   ```

3. After 5min upload a file  to the directory step2 created:

   ```bash
   curl -F "file=@example.txt" http://localhost:8888/logs/test/example.txt
   ```



4. Wait for the TTL to expire.

5. Attempt to access the file via the weed mount or filer webui.

**Expected behavior:**

The directory `/logs/test/` should persist until all contained files have expired and been deleted. Files should remain accessible until their individual TTLs have elapsed.

**Actual behavior:**

The `/logs/test/` directory is deleted once its TTL expires, even if it contains files that have not yet reached their TTL. This premature deletion prevents access to the remaining valid files.

**Proposed solution:**

Modify the `CreateEntry` function to set the TTL of directories to zero, ensuring that directories are not subject to TTL-based deletion. This change would allow directories to persist until all contained files have expired, maintaining consistent access to valid files.

**Additional context:**

This issue affects scenarios where path-specific TTLs are used to manage file lifecycles. The unintended deletion of directories does not remove the files themselves, but it makes them inaccessible through the file system interface since the parent directories no longer exist. This may cause confusion and operational issues, even though the underlying data still exists until its own TTL expires.

items.title: Fix filer GET error caused by incorrect database connection management
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?
This resolves filer errors like "Internal /buckets/XXX: find /buckets/XXX: context canceled" when using SQL filer store. The *sql.DB uses ctx from http.Request to create new connection, and then put it back to the connection pool. That means connections inside the pool are mostly unhealthy because the request context are cancelled just after http request finished.

# How are we solving the problem?
By uses sql.Conn instead of directly sql.DB. The sql.Conn are retrieved with context.Background(), while the later query still executes on request context, ensuring correct release logic.

# How is the PR tested?
Tested by manually stress testing, as that's a lifecycle problem making it hard to build unit tests.


# Checks
- [x] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [x] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

items.title: redis2: expire entries without destroying a concurrent recreate
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

The pre-existing race #10735 deliberately left open, with a worse outcome than the one it fixed: the logical-expiry branch in `ListDirectoryEntries` does an unconditional `DEL` of the value plus a bare `ZREM` of the member. A concurrent `InsertEntry` landing between the lister's `GET` and that `DEL` loses the freshly written value — not just an index member, the data. Its `ZAddNX` no-ops against the still-present member, so the recreate leaves neither value nor listing.

Stacked on #10743; review the last commit.

# How are we solving the problem?

The multi-key `MULTI`/Lua form is still off the table (`CROSSSLOT` under `redis_cluster2`, the value and index keys carry no hash tag), but the value delete only needs to be atomic against the value key itself, and single-key scripts are cluster-safe. The expiry branch now:

- re-reads the value and re-checks logical expiry on those exact bytes — a recreate that already landed is simply kept;
- deletes through a single-key compare-and-delete script, so the `DEL` fires only if the value still holds the bytes the decision was made on — a recreate that lands mid-flight survives untouched;
- removes the member through `removeOrphanedDirectoryListMember` instead of a bare `ZREM`, which restores the member if an insert races the removal, and reuses the not-found repair when the redis TTL won the race after all.

The expiry predicate moves into `isLogicallyExpired` so the loop and the recheck cannot drift apart. Costs one extra `GET` per expired entry, on the expiry path only.

# How is the PR tested?

Three new gated tests: end-to-end listing of a logically expired entry (value and member both gone, under both key prefixes — deterministic, no sleeps: `Crtime` an hour back with a 60s TTL keeps the physical key alive while logically expired), a recreate racing the expiry decision (value and member both survive), and the compare-and-delete script refusing mismatched bytes. Full suite passes with `-race` against a live Redis.

# What problem are we solving?
When using Redis store there are a lot of single commands sent to Redis sequentially. This causes many round trips and network IO wait.
For example for directories this produces a GET command for each child in the directory. Imagine a folder with a million files, it would sequentially execute 1 million GET commands.

Using the client-side pipelining feature to send all commands and get all their results in a single roundtrip.

items.title: fix: JTI replay protection
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

**CRITICAL Security Vulnerability**: JWT tokens in SeaweedFS S3 OIDC authentication can currently be reused unlimited times until expiration. If an attacker intercepts a valid JWT token (via MITM, log exposure, or compromised client), they can replay it repeatedly for the full token lifetime (typically 1 hour) to gain unauthorized access.

**Impact**:
- Stolen tokens provide unrestricted access until expiration
- No protection against replay attacks
- Violates defense-in-depth security principles

This PR implements JTI (JWT ID) claim tracking per RFC 7519 Section 4.1.7 to detect and reject replayed tokens.

---

# How are we solving the problem?

**Architecture**: Per-provider in-memory JTI cache with TTL-based expiration

**Implementation**:
1. Added optional `jtiReplayProtectionEnabled` config field (default: `true` - secure by default)
2. Added optional `jtiCacheMaxSize` config field (default: `10000` entries ≈ 1 MB)
3. Track seen JTI values in `sync.Map` with atomic `LoadOrStore()` to prevent TOCTOU races
4. Cache entries expire when token expires (TTL = `exp` claim + 5 min clock skew tolerance)
5. Background cleanup goroutine removes expired entries every 5 minutes
6. Graceful shutdown via `Shutdown(ctx)` method

**Key Security Features**:
- **Atomic insertion**: `sync.Map.LoadOrStore()` prevents concurrent replays (TOCTOU-safe)
- **Memory bounded**: Atomic counter with pre-check prevents DoS via JTI flooding
- **Clock skew tolerance**: 5-minute buffer matches JWT library behavior
- **Secure by default**: Enabled automatically, can be explicitly disabled if needed

**Backward Compatibility**:
- ✅ Tokens without JTI claims still accepted (warning logged)
- ✅ Feature can be disabled: `"jtiReplayProtectionEnabled": false`
- ✅ No breaking API changes
- ✅ Existing configs work without modification

**Example Configuration**:
```json
{
  "iam": {
    "providers": [{
      "type": "oidc",
      "name": "my-provider",
      "issuer": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0",
      "clientId": "my-client-id",
      "jwksUri": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/discovery/v2.0/keys",
      "jtiReplayProtectionEnabled": true,
      "jtiCacheMaxSize": 10000
    }]
  }
}
```

---

# How is the PR tested?

**Unit Tests** (7 comprehensive tests):
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTIReplayProtection` - Basic replay detection
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTIReplayProtectionDisabled` - Disabled mode works
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTIExpiration` - Clock skew and expiration handling
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTIReplayProtectionConcurrent` - 100 concurrent goroutines (race-free)
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTICacheMaxSize` - Memory bounds enforcement
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderJTICleanup` - Background cleanup verification
- ✅ `TestOIDCProviderShutdown` - Graceful shutdown

**Benchmarks** (performance validation):
- ✅ `BenchmarkJTIValidation` - Baseline performance
- ✅ `BenchmarkJTIValidationWithReplay` - Replay detection overhead
- ✅ `BenchmarkJTIValidationNoProtection` - Disabled mode performance

**Test Results**:
```bash
go test -v ./weed/iam/oidc -run "TestOIDCProviderJTI"  # All PASS ✅
go test -race ./weed/iam/oidc -run "TestOIDCProviderJTI"  # No JTI races ✅
go vet ./weed/iam/oidc/...  # PASS ✅
go test -bench=BenchmarkJTI ./weed/iam/oidc  # Negligible overhead ✅
```

**Race Condition Testing**:
- JTI code is completely race-free (verified with `-race` flag)
- Note: Existing JWKS race conditions are intentional (separate PR `feature/jwks-caching` will fix)

---

# Checks
- [x] I have added unit tests if possible.
- [ ] I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.
- [ ] All AI code review comments have been addressed.

# Checks for AI generated PRs
- [x] I have reviewed every line of code.
- [x] The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted.

**Describe the bug**
I have a single Master, Single Filer and a single Volume. I had setup Remote mount and was uploading the files in s3. The server having the volume crashed beyond recovery. Since I had the Gateway to Remote Object Storage setup, my assumption is that Local FS is a cache to the S3. and since cache can be volatile there should be no issue if the cache is cleared, With Actual files stored safely in S3. However to my surprise. I cannot access the files uploaded to s3 via seaweed. I am getting an error `operation LookupFileId 3,0da488208f failed, err: urls not found`. 

The file is present in both Filer UI and S3 Bucket. 

**System Setup**

Start the master, Volume and filer with below docker-compose file.

items.title: fix: jwks cache race condition
items.body:
# What problem are we solving?

  The OIDC provider's JWKS (JSON Web Key Set) cache had a critical race condition that could occur
  under high concurrent load:

  1. **Race condition on cache access:** Multiple goroutines could read/write jwksCache and jwksFetchedAt
  simultaneously without proper locking, causing data races detected by Go's race detector.
  2. **Duplicate concurrent fetches:** When JWKS cache expired, multiple concurrent token validation
  requests would all trigger separate HTTP calls to fetch JWKS from the provider, causing unnecessary
  load and potential rate limiting.
  3. **Use-after-unlock bugs:** The code returned pointers to JWK objects while holding a read lock, but
  the pointer could be invalidated after the lock was released if another goroutine updated the cache.

  # How are we solving the problem?

  The fix implements proper concurrency control with three key improvements:

  1. **RWMutex protection**: Added sync.RWMutex to protect all access to jwksCache and jwksFetchedAt,
  preventing data races.
  2. **Singleflight pattern**: Integrated golang.org/x/sync/singleflight to ensure only one JWKS fetch
  happens even when many concurrent requests need it. Other requests wait for the in-flight fetch to
  complete.
  3. **Lock-free HTTP calls**: Moved the HTTP request outside of any locks to prevent blocking all readers
   during slow network calls. Only the final cache update holds a write lock (very brief).
  4. **Defensive copying**: findAndCopyKey() returns a copy of the JWK, not a pointer to cached data,
  preventing use-after-unlock bugs.

  # How is the PR tested?

  Added comprehensive race condition tests in weed/iam/oidc/oidc_race_test.go:

  1. **TestJWKSCacheConcurrentRefresh**: Tests 50 concurrent token validations during:
    - Initial JWKS fetch (cold cache)
    - Cache expiration and refresh
    - Verifies only 1-5 fetches occur instead of 50
  2. **TestJWKSCacheIsolation:** Tests cache updates don't interfere with concurrent reads by simulating
  10 concurrent readers performing 20 validations each while JWKS updates happen.
  3. **Race detector validation**: 100 concurrent goroutines each performing 10 iterations to stress-test
  the locking implementation.

  All tests pass with go test -race without any race condition warnings.

  # Checks

  - I have added unit tests if possible.
  - I will add related wiki document changes and link to this PR after merging.

  # Checks for AI generated PRs

  - I have reviewed every line of code.
  - The PR is kept as minimum as possible. Large PRs would not be accepted.

  ---
  **Note**: The changes are minimal (85 lines of logic + 297 lines of tests) and focused solely on fixing
  the race condition without altering any functionality. All existing OIDC functionality remains
  unchanged.

items.title: S3: RenameObject accepts x-amz-client-token but does not implement idempotency
items.body:
`RenameObject` documents idempotency through `x-amz-client-token`, and the AWS SDKs auto-fill that header on every call (`OperationIdempotencyTokenAutoFill` in aws-sdk-go-v2). SeaweedFS accepts the header and ignores it.

Two gaps against the [documented contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/API/API_RenameObject.html):

- A rename that commits but whose response is lost returns `NoSuchKey` on the SDK's retry, instead of replaying the success. The source is already gone, so the retry cannot succeed on its own.
- Reusing a token with different parameters should return `IdempotentParameterMismatch`; it currently just performs the second rename.

Rejecting the header is not an option — the SDKs always send it, so every SDK caller would break. Accepting and ignoring it is what #10659 ships, with the limitation stated in the PR.

Implementing it properly means durable state the gateways share: token -> normalized request + result, TTL-expired, consulted before the move and written after it. A per-gateway in-memory cache would cover the common retry but behave non-deterministically across a fleet, which is arguably worse than a predictable 404. There is no client-token or idempotency infrastructure in the tree today, so this is a subsystem rather than a patch — and one that would serve any other operation wanting the same guarantee.

items.title: Complete data loss when using volume.tier.move after volume.tier.upload
items.body:
**Describe the bug**
When first uploading the data via `volume.tier.upload` e.g. with [rclone](https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/5853):
`volume.tier.upload -dest rclone -fullPercent=95 -quietFor=1s -keepLocalDatFile=false -collection=default`

and then moving the data to a different storage tier with:
`volume.tier.move -fromDiskType=hdd -toDiskType=hdd2 -quietFor=30s -fullPercent=95 -force -collectionPattern=* -toReplication=000`

**all of the data that was first moved by rclone will be wiped** because the dat file was not downloaded before moving the data to hdd2. Only the index files were moved during the `volume.tier.move` operation.

**System Setup**
- OS version: Ubuntu 22.04
- weed version: "chrislusf/seaweedfs:3.71_full" (rclone requires full version)

**Expected behavior**
Remote tier dat file should be downloaded before `volume.tier.move` operation.

**Screenshots**
hdd2 volume server says it has id=12 in remote storage:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/959860dc-4c80-487b-aaaa-81f3247d8f1b)

but only idx file is there:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f0ce040a-1cda-4c26-a00e-948c3ee76c2a)

and the remote storage box has been fully wiped (had ~3TB of data):
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/43f76e14-cf32-4a60-ba7c-7243fdaa149c)

Luckily, this was just ~3TB of test data, but when not being careful, this combination of commands can lead to 100% data loss.

items.title: Superblock and ".vif" files are not in sync
items.body:
As discovered in #4934 :

It looks like in order to determine the replication setting,  sometimes the superblock is used and sometimes the `.vif` 

For example, when a new volume file gets created, the replication setting and the TTL is stored in the superblock only.
The `.vif` file looks like this:
```
{
  "files": [],
  "version": 3,
  "replication": "",
  "BytesOffset": 4
}
```

When I manually change the replication setting using `volume.configure.replication -collectionPattern * -replication 010`, the `.vif` file is updated but the superblock is not. The volume server now uses the `.vif`:

```
{
  "files": [],
  "version": 3,
  "replication": "010",
  "BytesOffset": 4
}
```

If I delete the `.vif` and restart the volume server, the `.vif` gets recreated without the `replication` setting and the volume server uses the outdated setting that it gets from the superblock.


**System Setup**
- Ubuntu 22.04
- output of `weed version`: version 30GB 3.57 0f8168c0c928bba3d2f48b0680d3bdce9c617559 linux amd64


**Expected behavior**
`volume.configure.replication` changes both superblock and `.vif` files
